title: Bash Script Basics
subtitle: #!/bin/bash, variables, echo, read, exit codes, making scripts executable
author: KERNAL Team

content.code:
#!/bin/bash
# The shebang line tells the OS which interpreter to use
# #!/bin/bash  — bash
# #!/bin/sh    — POSIX sh (more portable, fewer features)
# #!/usr/bin/env bash  — find bash in PATH (recommended)

# Comment: lines starting with # are comments
echo "Hello, World!"

# Variables (no spaces around =)
NAME="Alice"
AGE=30
GREETING="Hello, $NAME! You are $AGE years old."
echo $GREETING

# Command substitution: capture command output
CURRENT_DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
FILE_COUNT=$(ls | wc -l)
echo "Today is $CURRENT_DATE, files: $FILE_COUNT"

# Read user input
echo -n "Enter your name: "   # -n: no newline
read USER_NAME
echo "Hello, $USER_NAME!"

content.text: Making scripts executable and running them

content.code:
# Make it executable
chmod +x hello.sh

# Run it
./hello.sh          # ./ required (not just hello.sh)
bash hello.sh       # run with bash explicitly (no chmod needed)
sh hello.sh         # run with sh

# Pass arguments to a script
./greet.sh Alice 30

# Inside the script, access arguments:
# $1 = first argument ('Alice')
# $2 = second argument ('30')
# $@ = all arguments
# $# = number of arguments
# $0 = script name

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Every command returns an exit code: 0 = success, 1-255 = error

ls /existing/path   # exit code 0
echo "Exit: $?"     # → 0

ls /nonexistent     # exit code 2
echo "Exit: $?"     # → 2 (non-zero = failure)

# exit: set script's exit code
if [ ! -f config.txt ]; then
  echo "Error: config.txt not found" >&2   # write error to stderr
  exit 1  # non-zero = failure
fi

echo "Config found"
exit 0   # success (optional — scripts exit 0 if they reach the end)

# Use exit codes in pipelines
if grep -q "ERROR" server.log; then
  echo "Errors found in log!"
fi
# grep returns 0 if match found, 1 if not, 2 if error

content.text: Start scripts with set -euo pipefail. -e exits on error, -u treats unset variables as errors, -o pipefail makes pipelines fail if any command fails. This catches bugs that would otherwise silently continue.

questions.question: What does the shebang line #!/usr/bin/env bash do?
options: It is a comment — all lines starting with # are ignored
It tells the OS to use bash as the interpreter, finding it via PATH
It imports bash functionality into sh
It sets the script's exit code to 0
questions.explanation: The shebang (#!) on the very first line tells the OS which interpreter to use to execute the script. /usr/bin/env bash uses the env command to find bash in the system PATH — more portable than #!/bin/bash (which only works if bash is installed at /bin/bash). Without a shebang, the OS uses the user's default shell, which may not be bash.

faq.q: Why do I need ./ before the script name?
faq.a: For security, the shell does not look in the current directory (.) when searching for commands — only in $PATH directories. ./hello.sh explicitly says 'run hello.sh in the current directory.' Without ./, the shell would search $PATH and not find hello.sh. You can add . to $PATH but it is a security risk (a malicious ls script in any directory you visit would run).

examples: Every GitHub Actions step that runs bash code is a mini-script — understanding bash scripting lets you write complex CI/CD logic
